text: Welcome to IT, Networking and Cloud Fundamentals, the first course on the DevOps Engineer path. Before you can automate a deployment or reason about an outage, you need a solid mental model of what a computer actually is. This lesson builds that model from the ground up.

Strip away everything else, and a computer is four physical pieces working together. The CPU executes instructions, billions of times per second. RAM is fast, temporary workspace that disappears when the power goes off. Storage is the slower, permanent home for files and programs. And the network interface is what lets the machine talk to other machines at all.

The operating system sits directly on top of that hardware and manages it for everything else. It schedules which program gets the CPU and for how long, so many programs appear to run at once. It hands out and reclaims RAM, so one program can't grab all the memory on the machine. And it gives every program a consistent way to read a file or reach the network, without that program needing to know the hardware details underneath.

Hold this three-layer picture in your head: applications like a browser or a point-of-sale app run through the operating system, never touching hardware directly, and the operating system manages the hardware underneath. At Northbridge Retail, that's a Linux-based OS on every checkout terminal and Windows laptops in the corporate office — different choices, same three layers.
Hardware, operating system, software — that's the lens for the rest of this course. Up next, lesson two: processes, memory, and storage in more depth.
